question: Nuclear energy generates 25 % of the EU’s electricity and provides more than 900 000 jobs along its value chain. While these aspects were finally acknowledged by the Commission, its draft nuclear illustrative programme (‘PINC’) fails to provide answers to the most pressing challenges the sector is facing.

For example, the draft PINC contains no concrete policy measures to facilitate the nuclear expansion that is necessary to achieve production targets. Furthermore, it fails to put nuclear energy on an equal footing with other clean energy technologies. Finally, the draft PINC includes no proposals to facilitate the access of nuclear energy projects to public and private financing.
We believe that, in its current form, the draft PINC fails to provide the necessary positive incentives for the use of nuclear energy. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission intend to complement the programme with a strategic action plan addressing these issues?
How does the Commission plan to ensure that the principle of technology neutrality is respected in its upcoming legislative initiatives?
Is the Commission ready to engage in a constructive dialogue with the EU nuclear alliance and the relevant industrial stakeholders concerning the future of nuclear energy in the EU?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain (PfE).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.3.2026) In line with Article 40 of the Euratom Treaty, the eighth Nuclear Illustrative Programme (PINC)1 provides an up-to-date, fact-based overview of nuclear development trends, challenges and investment needs across the EU to achieve Member States plans2, in line with decarbonisation targets and the Clean Industrial Deal goals.

Upcoming initiatives, such as the Clean Energy Investment Strategy and the Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) Strategy will build on the PINC and aim to address the identified gaps by supporting Member States, industry and regulators. All zero and low carbon energy solutions are needed to decarbonise the energy system by 20403.

Thus, current and upcoming policy initiatives incorporate the principle of technological neutrality. The Commission will provide guidance to Member States on the design of contracts for difference, their combination with power purchase agreements, thereby supporting Member States in designing support schemes for nuclear installations in a technology-neutral way.

The Commission remains committed to a constructive, inclusive dialogue with all Member States, including those in the Nuclear Alliance, and with all relevant stakeholders, including industrial stakeholders particularly engaged in nuclear energy4.

euratom-treaty_en. 2 Delivering on Member States’ plans will require significant investments estimated at EUR 241 billion until 2050 covering the newbuild of large-scale reactors and lifetime extensions (‘base case scenario’ with 109 GW capacity). 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52024DC0063. 4 e.g. the Commissioner for Energy and Housing participated in a call with the Nuclear Alliance on 18 February 2025 and hosted an industry dialogue with nuclear stakeholders on 7 April 2025.
